title: What changed when my agents stopped sharing a context
excerpt: Splitting one long prompt into a writer, a reviewer and a fact-checker made the drafts better and the pipeline slower. Here is where the time went.
content:
Every agent pipeline starts the same way: one model, one prompt, one happy path. The trouble begins when the second agent arrives and the two of them have to agree on what *done* means.[^1]

This post walks through what changed when the blog's writer, reviewer and fact-checker stopped sharing a single context and started handing work to each other.

## Why one context stopped working

A single context is cheap to reason about. Every step can see every earlier step, so nothing is ever lost in a hand-off. It is also the reason the drafts got worse as they got longer: the reviewer was grading text it had partly written itself.[^2]

Splitting the work meant each agent saw only what it needed. The writer saw the brief and the sources. The reviewer saw the draft and the rubric. The fact-checker saw claims, one at a time, and nothing else.

> The fastest way to make an agent honest is to stop showing it its own work.

## The hand-off format

Each hand-off is a small JSON document rather than free text. That sounds bureaucratic, but it is what lets a later step reject an earlier one without arguing about tone.

```ts
type Handoff = {
  stage: "draft" | "review" | "factcheck";
  input: string;
  verdict?: "pass" | "revise";
  notes: string[];
};
```

The reviewer can return `revise` with notes, and the writer gets exactly those notes back, not the reviewer's whole transcript.[^3]

## What it cost

Three agents cost more tokens than one, but less than you would expect. Most of the reviewer's and fact-checker's input is short, and the writer's second pass is usually a small edit rather than a rewrite.

The bigger cost was latency. A draft that took forty seconds now takes about two minutes, because the stages run one after another. For a blog that publishes a few times a week, that trade was easy.

## What I would do differently

I would add the fact-checker first, not last. It caught more real problems than the reviewer did, and it is the simplest of the three to build.

[^1]: In practice "done" meant three different things: the writer thought it meant "long enough", the reviewer "on topic", and the fact-checker "nothing false".
[^2]: This is the same reason code review works better when the reviewer did not write the code.
[^3]: Keeping the notes short also keeps the writer's context small, which matters more than the token count suggests.
